title: Dhruva, the boy who became the pole star
hookLine: a five-year-old's prayer holds so steady that Vishnu sets him in the sky, and it's why a Hindu couple is shown the pole star
last: THE WASP — YOU BECOME WHAT YOU DWELL ON.

lines: A BOY PULLED OFF A LAP.
cards: The Bhagavata tells of a boy named Dhruva. He's five. He climbs onto his father the king's lap, and his stepmother pulls him off: if you wanted that lap, she says, you should have been born to me.
He runs to his mother, crying. She doesn't fight back. She tells him only the Lord can give him a place no one can take.
So the five-year-old walks into the forest to find the Lord.

teach.b: On the way, the sage Narada tests him: you're a child, go home. Dhruva won't. So Narada gives him a mantra, om namo bhagavate vasudevaya, and a way to sit.
Dhruva prays by the Yamuna for months, eating less and less, until he stands on one foot, and the story says the whole world feels his weight. Vishnu comes.
And here's the turn: Dhruva finds he no longer wants what he came for. He went looking for a lap and found the Lord.
Vishnu gives him a place anyway, the star that never moves, the one point the whole night sky turns around. Dhruva means fixed, steady.
That's the teaching: in Hinduism, steadiness is itself devotion, and God answers a prayer that doesn't move, even a child's. You can see it at a Hindu wedding.
In many weddings, the priest shows the couple the pole star, Dhruva, as a picture of a marriage that holds. Now Patanjali points samyama at the sky. Sutra 3.26, on the sun: knowledge of the worlds.
3.27, on the moon: how the stars are arranged.

teach.h: THE WEDDING: SHOWN THE POLE STAR.
teach.b: 3.28, on the pole star: how they move.
Fix on the one point that doesn't move, and you can read the motion of everything else. Then 3.29 comes down to the body's own center, the navel.
It's why so many Hindus keep one prayer every single day, the way Dhruva kept his mantra.
When a week won't stop moving, that prayer is the point that doesn't.

how: Dhruva's story is commonly told to Hindu children, Narada's twelve-syllable mantra to Vishnu is widely chanted, and in many Hindu weddings the couple is shown the pole star as a sign of a steady marriage; teachers of the Yoga Sutras read 3.26–3.29 as samyama moving from the sky to the body's center.

o: the pole star, the point the night turns around
the morning star that rises just before dawn
a sage who drew the first map of the heavens

games.q: Dhruva and his star — tap the pairs.
p: a mantra and a way to sit

s: when Vishnu appeared, Dhruva still wanted his father's throne most of all
in the Bhagavata he finds he no longer wants what he came for; he'd found the Lord.
in many Hindu weddings the couple is shown the pole star
dhruva, the steady star, as a picture of a marriage that holds.
samyama on the moon gives knowledge of the worlds
the moon gives the stars' arrangement; the sun gives the worlds.

games.q: a friend says prayer is just asking God for stuff. what does Dhruva's story say?
o: he went asking for a lap, kept praying without moving, and found God, whom he wanted more than what he'd asked for.
prayer works only if you ask for something big enough.
a child's prayer doesn't count until they're grown.
games.why: Dhruva came for his father's lap and found the Lord. in Hinduism steady devotion is itself the gift, and God answers it, even from a five-year-old.

practice: Let your attention rest on one point. If you pray, make it the name Narada gave Dhruva, om namo bhagavate vasudevaya, said slowly. If you don't, make it the navel, rising and falling with the breath.
Thoughts will move around it like the night sky turning. You don't have to stop them. Stay with the one point, and watch the rest move.

wordCard.voice: Dhruva: fixed, steady. The pole star, and the boy who became it, with a prayer that didn't move.

orig.note: Sanskrit dhruva: fixed, steady; the pole star, and the name of the boy in the Puranas who became it.

carryVoice: Your line: dhruva, devotion that doesn't move. A child's steady prayer, set in the sky. Rest easy.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 4.8–4.9 (Dhruva; Narada's twelve-syllable mantra at 4.8.54; Dhruva's regret at having asked for a kingdom)
